title: How would you approach terrain materials and shading for environment?
author: Just-Huckleberry-282
selftext:
I’m building a cycling app with an indoor training/racing mode that runs through 3D worlds in Three.js. It’s not really a game, but this part of the product has effectively become one from a rendering perspective.

The physics and rider systems are working well, but I’m struggling to establish a convincing environment—particularly the terrain shading and material system. Individual components can look acceptable in isolation, but once combined, the terrain still tends to read as flat, synthetic, overly faceted, or visually disconnected from the road.

The clip shows the current state.

Tiled terrain textures have been a particular problem. The assets I’ve tried either repeat visibly, introduce unwanted colour and contrast, operate at the wrong spatial scale, or fight the low-poly terrain forms. Removing them solves the repetition but leaves the terrain looking sterile and synthetic.

The stack is Three.js/WebGL, with real elevation data driving the terrain. I’ve used AI heavily during implementation and iteration, but not with the expectation that it can generate the final look.

If you’ve solved something similar, I’d really appreciate suggestions:

* How would you structure terrain detail across macro, meso and micro scales?
* Would you keep albedo mostly procedural/low-frequency and use tiling only for roughness and subtle normals?
* What techniques work well for breaking texture repetition across large terrain in Three.js/WebGL?
* How do you preserve readable terrain relief without exposing the mesh triangulation?
* How would you approach lighting and atmospheric depth?
* How do you make the road and shoulders feel embedded rather than layered on top?
* At what point would you conclude that the remaining problem is terrain geometry rather than materials?

I’ve been staring at it for too long and may be optimizing the wrong layer at this point.

Happy to share implementation details

comments.author: joeld42
comments.body:
Hey, I'm a graphics programmer and a Zwift user, i'd love to test out your game. Also check out BikeTerra which is doing a similar thing.

To answer your questions, usually terrain is textured with "triplanar mapping" where you repeat a texture projecting it onto the X Y or Z axis so that it limits stretching. You also should use "detail normal maps" which are repeated normal maps at a higher frequency for close terrain.

Often terrain engines will support vertex color blending to allow 4 or 8 different terrain textures to be blended between. You can also use vertex color for hue variation, e.g. make the ground texture more greyish and blend in some greens, browns and yellows from the vertex color. Tricky to get right but can look really good when it works. Another good trick is to reuse the same texture at a different scale past a certain distance, doesn't work with all textures but  with a lot of landscape  There are some good youtube videos from Jason Booth about "Microsplat" terrain texture solution for Unity, he does a good job explaining how they work and you might be able to re-use some of those techniques.

  
More advanced techniques (now we're in open world game territory) are using decals and vegetation systems to cover most of the terrain and relying on the terrain just for middle distance and background, and building the parts near the player out of terrain chunks (meshes) rather than using elevation terrain. These might not be options if you're building the terrain on the fly but worth experimenting.

Feel free to DM me or reach out -- doing a procedural bike scenery project is a project I've always wanted to do but have too many other projects and I'd be happy to help out.

replies.author: joeld42
replies.body:
Oh yeah, one more trick that is pretty simple, is to repeat the texture but in an irregular way. There's a good article here with some examples: [https://iquilezles.org/articles/texturerepetition/](https://iquilezles.org/articles/texturerepetition/)   
Combine this with some scaling based on distance and you can pretty nice terrain textures.

replies.author: Just-Huckleberry-282
replies.body: thanks. much appreciated, good article indeed.

replies.author: Just-Huckleberry-282
replies.body:
Thanks man, really appreciate it. I’ll dig into MicroSplat and the techniques you mentioned, especially detail normals, terrain texture blending and reusing textures at different scales.

I’m a software engineer by trade, but rendering definitely isn’t my area of expertise. I’m trying to accelerate my learning enough to understand the fundamentals and steer the AI properly, rather than blindly asking it to make things look better.

The app is [gritmo.net](https://gritmo.net) and it’s still very much in alpha, but by all means feel free to explore. Feedback would be incredibly useful, especially from someone who is both a graphics programmer and a Zwift user :)

The indoor training side is functional and should work with FTMS trainers. I’ve also implemented automatic virtual shifting for single-cog setups. It’s a little gimmicky, but fun to experiment with.

Thanks again for the offer. I’ll definitely reach out when I inevitably hit another wall on the rendering side 🙂
